item.title: 5 Open-World RPGs Everyone Should Play To Completion
item.description:
Open-world RPGs consume lives. The "short" titles require roughly 15 hours, while the normal-length ones can easily demand 50 hours to reach the end of their stories. As great as they are, nobody really needs to complete Elden Ring or Skyrim , and many of the genre's legendary games shine the brightest when players decide to simply exist within their worlds indefinitely. However, a small handful of open-world RPGs really demand to be completed, at least when it comes to their main content.

I am the type of person who moves on once I stop having fun with a game, and that is especially true for open-world RPGs that seem to last forever and a day. Often, a campaign's final act is not worth plowing through hours of exhaustion, but exceptions certainly exist. If you feel your interest in these games starting to wane, I recommend pushing through the story to reach the end.

"Completion" means finishing the story and not "completing everything in the game."

Cyberpunk 2077 Ends Better Than It Starts

V And Johnny's Dynamic Anchors The Entire Campaign, Right Up To The Final Moments

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt might seem like an obvious pick for this article, but its length makes it a hard sell and its story climax doesn't quite feel as urgent as it should, despite a lot being on the line. Comparatively, Cyberpunk 2077 takes you on a far more condensed journey, one with a ticking clock that drives everything forward. Night City doesn't reward aimless wandering; instead, it acts as a meat grinder that tests a person's ideals, instincts, and willingness to shed their humanity.

Story-wise, the campaign reaches its peak during the final act, which comes with a variety of endings that let you determine how V exits the stage. Beyond just seeing how it all ends for the protagonist, you need to experience the full story to see Johnny Silverhand's complete character arc and the culmination of his relationship with V, the latter of which serves as the cornerstone of the whole game.

Gameplay-wise, Cyberpunk 2077 's progression system opens up so many possibilities that you will be able to create some absolutely wild (and overpowered) versions of V, letting you terrorize Night City as the ultimate cyberware powerhouse.

8 Best RPGs That Get Better As You Play, Ranked

These excellent RPGs are good from the start, but they continue to get better and better as players delve into their intricate worlds.

6
By Ritwik Mitra

Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen Literally Needs To Be Completed

Otherwise, You Don't Get To The Best Part!

Let's go for something a bit different. Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen needs to be completed for the simple fact that its best part, Bitterblack Isle, takes place after the base game's ending. Once the story concludes, the Dark Arisen expansion kicks in, introducing an endgame dungeon that actually makes use of all of Dragon's Dogma ​​​​​​'s deep RPG systems.

Unlike the vanilla content, which becomes way too easy after a few hours, Bitterblack Isle requires you to optimize your stats, augments, and Pawns, as anything less will almost certainly result in death. DD has a fantastic class/Vocation system that provides plenty of room to experiment, and the post-game content lets you push your capabilities to the max.

Also, the combat system gets better as you spend more time with it.

Nier: Automata Ends So Many Times Before It Really Ends

It's Not Over Until It's Truly Over

Nier: Automata doesn't end until you get into one of the most absurd bullet-hell fights in gaming history. Famously, Yoko Taro split the campaign into alphabetical routes, with the first path concluding with "Ending A." However, the subsequent routes aren't replays but rather the next chapters in the story; basically, shutting down the game after "Ending A" would be like turning off Red Dead Redemption 2 after completing "Chapter 2."

Nier: Automata 's story reaches its true completion with "Ending E," which requires players to "restart" the campaign four times. Routes C and D are essentially full-length sequels to Routes A and B, introducing a new protagonist and the deterioration of a former lead. Route E brings everything to an end with one of the more unusual meta questions in gaming.

6 Hardest Japanese Open-World RPGs, Ranked

While not impossible to beat, these RPGs are some of the hardest games in their genre. The fact that they're open-world just amplifies the difficulty

4
By Tristan Jurkovich

Fallout: New Vegas Remembers Who You Are And What You Did

If You Set Up A Row Of Dominoes, You Need To Knock Them Down

I love a good Bethesda RPG, but their narrative endings often feel like afterthoughts that just exist because they need to. Skyrim is probably the most obvious example, but the endings of Fallout 3 and 4 are rushed and disconnected from the player's choices, which is especially disappointing, given the legacy of the original isometric games. Obsidian's Fallout: New Vegas does not have this problem.

Unlike so many open-world RPGs that end with cinematic cutscenes that barely seem to link to your last 30 hours of gameplay, New Vegas builds on everything that came before, creating a domino effect where every minor settlement, loyalty mission, and faction skirmish impacts the world's state. Quitting before the Second Battle of Hoover Dam robs Mojave of its connective tissue, reducing Obsidian's consequential design to isolated side quests and dialogue choices.

Yakuza: Like a Dragon's Ending Amplifies The Rest Of The Game

An Open-World RPG That Ends On A Real High Note

Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio's pivot of a beloved franchise from action to turn-based combat was one heck of a gamble, but the developer proved to be a more-than-capable student of the house that Dragon Quest built. All entries in the series are fairly long, but Yakuza: Like a Dragon will almost certainly require about 50 hours, especially since it throws in a rather annoying wall during "Chapter 12" that requires serious grinding.

Although great from the start, the story not only reaches a beautiful crescendo in its final hours, but also injects a heightened sense of tragedy that really amplifies the emotional weight. If you stop around Chapter 10, you will have played a fun, albeit silly, open-world RPG that pays tribute to the turn-based greats. By finishing the campaign, you will have experienced an all-time great story that gives satisfying conclusions to all the main characters, including your party members.

item.title: Fable’s Story Length Praised by Gamers
item.description:
Fable 's main story length has officially been revealed, and gamers are largely satisfied with the runtime. Playground Games and Xbox recently shared more details about Fable 's story at Gamescom 2026, including how long players can expect to take to beat it. With how drastically different RPG lengths can be, knowing the length of Fable 's story ahead of time can help players manage their expectations.

After being delayed out of 2026, Fable will finally be released on February 23, 2027, making it the first new entry in the franchise in over a decade. As such, there are some high expectations for the fantasy RPG to meet, including the amount of content contained within its total runtime. Luckily, fans looking for a solid amount to do within Fable 's world of Albion will be happy to hear that the game's main story length is quite sizable, and that's just a slice of the total pie.

February 2027's New Game Releases Look Like September 2026 All Over Again

September is packed with a wild number of great-looking games, and February 2027 is quickly finding itself in the same situation.

By LB Beistad

Fable Will Take Roughly 15-20 Hours to Beat the Main Story

Revealed during a Q&A session at Gamescom and reported by Polygon, Fable 's associate game director Will Kennedy said that it will take players around 15-20 hours to complete the main quest. If this number is accurate, it would make this game the longest in the Fable franchise, even if it doesn't compare to other fantasy RPGs like The Elder Scrolls franchise or behemoths like Baldur's Gate 3 . For comparison, the past entries in the Fable series have had main stories that lasted less than 15 hours total.

  • Fable (2004) — 12.5 Hours
  • Fable 2 (2008) — 13 Hours
  • Fable 3 (2010) — 13.5 Hours

In a post reacting to this news on the Fable subreddit, gamers responded with generally favorable opinions on the campaign length. As a comment by user Grouchy-Fill1675 puts it, "As an almost 40-year-old husband and father, this doesn't bother me in the slightest." Other users shared this sentiment, expressing that a 15-20-hour story for an RPG is perfect when super-long games like Persona 5 and Baldur's Gate 3 can get overwhelming. Other users pointed out that with Fable 's morality system, this length can essentially be doubled for one good and one evil playthrough.

However, there is much more to Fable than just the main campaign, and Kennedy goes on to explain that there is another 15-20 hours of side content for players to engage with. As an open-world RPG, Fable allows players to get lost in the world of Albion and explore every nook and cranny to their heart's content, expanding the game's runtime by as much or as little as they'd like. Fable will also feature a life system that essentially makes the game limitless depending on how much players want to commit to roleplaying within this world.

Fable’s Story Length Praised by Gamers
Official New Fable Event Confirmed for August 26
Fable Just Got a 1-2 Punch of Very Bad News
Fable Features 1000 Romanceable and "Handcrafted" NPCs

Although Fable may not be the massive RPG experience that some fans are hoping for, a modest story length with an equal helping of side content seems to be sitting right with the majority of fans. The quality of Fable 's story and gameplay is likely going to be the difference-maker more so than the quantity. And with the return of fan-favorite villain Jack of Blades along with immersive features like over 1000 romanceable NPCs, players will likely be able to squeeze more than enough quality hours of gameplay out of Fable to make the game worth the purchase.

item.title: How to Fish: How to Catch Triggerfish
item.description:
How to Fish has five islands and more than 40 creatures to catch, but finding some of them can be a real pain. The Triggerfish is one of those creatures, especially if you don’t know which bait to use or where to look for it. If you are trying to add the Triggerfish to your creature collection in How to Fish , here’s everything you need to know.

How to Catch an Endangered Creature for the Tourist in How to Fish

The tourist on the third island wants an endangered creature in How to Fish. Here’s how to complete his quest.

By Umama Ali

How to Catch the Triggerfish in How to Fish

  • The Triggerfish is found on the Forest Island, and you'll require the Fishing Rod and Beginner Lure.

To catch the Triggerfish, you will first need to leave the Lighthouse island by completing the Who Stole My Beer quest, kill the Spider Crab, and get the boat keys from the Lighthouse Keeper. Then take the boat to the Forest island.

Once you get there, you will need to go to the shop and buy the Fishing Rod . The Crab Fishing Rod from the Lighthouse won’t work for catching Triggerfish. You will also need the Beginner Lure , which is the only bait that works for this fish. It costs just $3, and you can use it to catch several other creatures in Forest as well, including Perch, Pike, and Goldfish.

Once you have the right fishing rod and lure, go to the water and cast your line. Wait for a fish to bite, then reel it in. You may need to try a few times because the Fishing Rod and Beginner Lure can also catch other creatures. Keep fishing, and you should eventually get a Triggerfish. There’s also a chance of catching the rarer Drip Triggerfish, which sells for more money.

Once you catch a Triggerfish, you will have to bring it back onto the island and kill it with any weapon. You can then sell it to the shopkeeper for $18 or eat it to restore your energy. The Drip Triggerfish sells for $33.

item.title: How To Unlock Secret Ending in Big Walk
item.description:
Even if you’ve reached the Big Goodbye in Big Walk , the journey is not quite over. The game has a second ending hidden behind its toughest completion requirement, and reaching it takes more than simply finishing the main story.

There’s another secret ending that requires you to complete the normal ending first and then complete seven post-game purple puzzles . It’s more demanding, but if you’re someone who wants to experience the true ending and get the Big Game achievement, read on to learn how to unlock Big Walk ’s secret ending.

How Long to Beat Big Walk

Wondering how long it would take you and your friends to beat Big Walk? Here’s what you need to know.

By Usama Ali

How Many Endings Does Big Walk Have?

Big Walk has two endings. The first is the normal ending, known as Big Goodbye, and happens after reaching the giant black sphere and completing the puzzles there.

The second is the secret or true ending. It is tied to the Big Game achievement and requires 100% completion. Unlike the first ending, this one requires going back through the world and finishing content that may have been skipped during the initial playthrough.

How To Unlock Secret Ending in Big Walk

To unlock the secret ending, you’ll first need to progress through the main game by completing the colored towers and collecting enough puzzle rewards to unlock the Black Tower .

Inside the Black Tower, complete the required puzzles and get the Black Key. Take the key to the Wall and use it to open the way forward. Beyond the Wall is the giant black sphere. Reach it and complete the puzzles in this area to trigger the first ending and roll the credits.

This unlocks the Big Goodbye achievement and moves the game into its post-game phase. Once the credits finish, return to the map room and start checking for unfinished puzzles .

The map in the Map Room does a lot more than you'd expect. It tracks every puzzle, shows your progress, and even lets you know if you've completed a puzzle, but the gourd is still there. Here's the quick breakdown: A gourd with no flag means it's incomplete. If it's tilted, you've finished it, but the gourd might still be there or waiting for you in the lost and found at the start.

Big Walk lets players reach the first ending without solving every puzzle, so it is possible to have lots of challenges left behind. Those unfinished puzzles count against the 100% completion requirement.

So, go back through the areas already visited and finish anything that was previously bypassed. This is also a good time to make sure the rewards from completed puzzles have actually been delivered where required.

Complete the Seven Purple Puzzles

The biggest part of the post-game cleanup is completing the seven purple puzzles. The purple puzzles become available after the first ending and are designed as harder versions of puzzle mechanics encountered during the main game.

  • The seven purple puzzles are part of the final completion requirement, so finishing the regular puzzles alone is not enough.
  • The purple puzzle area can be reached through the post-game content near the far eastern chairlift station. Once the challenges have been completed, the resulting purple collectibles can be added to the rest of the required rewards.
  • After completing the missed puzzles and all seven purple puzzles, take the remaining collectibles back to the green building near the tutorial and map area. Once the required set has been delivered, you will get the White Key.

The White Key is needed to access the secret ending. If the White Key does not appear, check the puzzle rewards again. Missing even one required puzzle can prevent the final collection from being completed.

Unlock the Secret Ending

  • With the White Key in hand, return to the area where the Big Walk began. Look for the small black sphere on the wall. After reaching the required completion percentage, this sphere will be split into two halves, revealing a hidden entrance between them.
  • Approach the opening between the two halves of the broken black sphere and use the White Key.
  • The entrance leads downstairs into a small hidden theater. This area begins the final sequence of the Big Walk and confirms that the required completion has been reached. Continue through the sequence until the curtain opens.
  • After entering the hidden theater, follow the sequence all the way through. Eventually, the group reaches the final area and is encouraged to separate from one another as the world begins to fill with light.
  • Completing this sequence finishes Big Walk . The Big Game achievement, which is described as completely finishing the game, should unlock once the true ending is completed. This is the secret ending of the Big Walk.

Can The Secret Ending Be Unlocked Without The First Ending?

No. The first ending needs to be completed before the seven purple post-game puzzles become available.

Once the credits roll, continue using the same save and begin cleaning up the unfinished content. There is no need to start a new game just to pursue the true ending.

FAQs

How many endings are there in Big Walk?

Big Walk has two endings. The first is the normal ending, which unlocks the Big Goodbye achievement. The second is the secret or true ending, which unlocks Big Game after reaching 100 percent completion.

Do all puzzles need to be completed for the secret ending?

Yes. Every puzzle needs to be completed, including challenges that were skipped during the main playthrough and all seven purple puzzles that appear after the first ending.

Is There A Third Ending In Big Walk?

No. Big Walk has only two endings.

Related Guides

If you need help with some more Big Walk puzzles, check out these guides:

  • Big Walk Microphone Puzzle Guide
  • Big Walk: Telescope Gestures Puzzle (Red Tower) Guide
  • Big Walk Blue Tower Solution & How to Ride the Train (Big Ride Achievement)
  • Big Walk: How to Solve the Invisible Symbols Puzzle (Blue Tower)
  • Big Walk: How to Solve Green Flare Puzzle (Blue Tower)
  • Big Walk Green Chair Headphone Puzzle Guide
  • Big Walk: All Tools & Items
